newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - W.Africa-Asia oil sales show big yr/yr gains.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - W.Africa-Asia oil sales show big yr/yr gains.

text.p: Sporadic waves of West African crude oil into Asian markets are no big surprise these days. But a look at the burgeoning trade on a long-term basis may raise some eyebrows.

Estimates vary, but year-to-date eastbound flows of the light, sweet grades from Nigeria, Angola, Gabon, Congo and Equatorial Guinea may have jumped by as much 30 percent from year-ago levels, and by as much a 75 percent over 1995 figures.

Gains of that sort, analysts say, prove that what was once just a "swing" trade -- with Africa's dated Brent-related grades flooding into Asia only when Asian benchmark Dubai grew costly enough relative to Brent to make African barrels a shrewd alternative -- is becoming more and more a market unto its own.

Because the best historical data on the trade comes from reported tanker fixings, which offer representative but incomplete lists of overall liftings, estimates differ as to exactly how quickly trade is growing.
But all signs point in the same direction.

According to London-based shipping consultants Richardson Lawrie, 1997 flows already average some 770,000 barrels per day (bpd) through May. The figure marks a 30.4 percent jump over the 590,000 bpd level seen in the first five months of 1996.

The London-based research team of tanker broker Simpson, Spence and Young (SSY), meanwhile, estimates year-to-date eastbound West African fixings at 805,000 bpd, up 12.8 percent over the same period last year, but higher than first-half 1995 by a whopping 79 percent.

While it is agreed that the Brent/Dubai spread is still the most sensitive variable in the West African equation on a month-to month basis, analysts say more basic fundamentals are behind the big year-on-year gains.

"Asia's appetite for Africa's light sweet grades has certainly been sustained over the last six months, but factors like shipping economics and changing trade patterns shape the bigger picture," said Mark Jenkins, SSY's director of research.

"Rising North Sea production and a growing U.S. leaning toward shorter-haul barrels are leaving less room for West African in the Atlantic basin. But Asia is happy to take the West African as an alternative to regional grades," he added.
Consultants Richardson Lawrie note that the relative affordability of shipping routes east of West Africa is also increasing trade.

"The typical trip around the Cape of Good Hope to South Korea takes 33 days, versus 30 to the U.S. Gulf. But in an Asian journey, a second cargo can be picked up in the Middle East for backhaul to Mediterranean markets," said an analyst with the firm.
"That means you can minimize the number of days your tanker is empty in the overall journey," he added.

Since January 1995, South Korea, whose tightened product specifications and limited refinery sophistication have made West Africa's low-sulphur barrels a quick fix, leads overall purchases of the grades, with 22.6 percent of total Asian buying.
Next is India, with 21.8 percent of sales, and Taiwan, with 20.6 percent, according to SSY figures.

China played a substantial role with 12.2 percent, with Singapore, Indonesia, and Japan taking single digit shares, and Australia and the Philippines chiming in for purchases worth less than one percent of the total.
